posts:
El Dorado is open.

It's a virtual world built on Swop. It's live in beta right now, and you can be inside it in about a minute.

https://www.swopme.co/eldorado

Getting in, start to finish:

1. Open swopme.co/eldorado
2. Sign in with your swop.id
3. Approve it in the Swop app — Wallet settings → Wallet connections → scan

That's it. No new account. No password to invent.

Got a headset? You never type a password with a controller.

Sign in on your phone, then enter the short code the headset shows you.

Then you're standing in it rather than looking at it.

Now the bit that makes it different from every virtual world you've been in.

In almost every game you've played, you don't own your stuff. You hold a licence to use it. The terms usually say so outright.

The publisher can close your account. Your inventory goes with it — not because anyone stole it, but because it was never in your hands.

It lived in their database. Your account was just the key.

Most also forbid selling or moving items outside their systems.

So the way out is controlled by the same people who control the way in.

The clearest example isn't an economy. It's a city.

Some developers rebuilt GTA III and Vice City from the outside, so they'd run properly on modern machines.

The projects shipped no game content. You had to own the original game for them to work at all.

They were taken down anyway.
DMCA notice, Feb 2021 — GitHub pulls the code. Counter-notice brings a fork back. Lawsuit that September. Down again in October. The next month, Take-Two ships its own remasters. Later settled.

Open the original repo today and you get:

“451 — Unavailable for Legal Reasons”

An error code originally meant for censorship. We checked the morning we published.

Take either side of that fight. The bit that matters is simpler:

Everyone who bought that game only ever had a licence to it. The city they drove around in existed because someone else allowed it to.

That's the normal condition of virtual worlds.

In El Dorado you arrive holding your own keys.

Swop is fully self-custodial — keys are generated and held on your device, and Swop never holds them.

Your way in is something you control, not an account someone can switch off.

Three practical things that follow:

No buying a token before you can act — transactions are gas-sponsored and Swop absorbs the fee.

It isn't trapped in one world — same wallet across Solana, Ethereum, Base and Polygon.
And losing your phone isn't losing anything. Log in with your email on a new phone and your wallet comes back. You can also export your key and open your assets in a totally different wallet.

What we're NOT claiming:

Self-custody isn't legal ownership. It changes what can be done to your ACCESS — can't be quietly frozen, not stuck in one platform's trading system.

It doesn't settle your legal rights in an item. That depends on terms and jurisdiction.

Anyone telling you a wallet turns a game item into property in the legal sense is skipping a step.

Also worth saying plainly: Swop has not commissioned a third-party security audit to date. Weigh that before you bring much into a beta.

And it IS a beta. Literally, not as a legal cushion.

Things will change under you. Some will break. Features will move.

Improvements ship EVERY WEEK — we'd rather build it in front of you than later.
Beta describes the state of the software. It doesn't move the consequences of rough edges onto you. If something behaves badly in there, that's ours to fix.

Come in.

swopme.co/eldorado — bring a swop.id, or claim one in the Swop app on the way.

https://www.swopme.co/blog/el-dorado-virtual-world-beta
